title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a design problem in AI in education: how K-12 learning should be designed when AI is introduced not just as a tool, but as a collaborative learning agent. The authors argue that while AI is increasingly discussed in schools, there is little guidance for teachers on what curriculum, interaction supports, and learning environments are needed for effective student-AI collaboration (SAC). The study asks four questions about what curriculum is needed, what supports are needed for student-AI interaction, what environments should be established, and how SAC may evolve over time.

The study uses in-depth semi-structured interviews with 10 Korean teachers who were identified as leading practitioners in AI in education. Participants came from primary and secondary schools involved in software-leading schools, AI pilot schools, or AI convergence curriculum-oriented high schools. Using thematic analysis informed by a distributed cognition framework, the authors developed themes around SAC design. Teachers emphasized learning goals such as higher-order thinking, digital capacity, social capacity, and subject-matter knowledge building. They recommended interdisciplinary learning, authentic problem solving, and creative tasks, along with process-oriented assessment and assessment of collaboration performance.

The paper also identifies supports needed for student-AI interaction. Teachers said students need instruction in AI principles, data literacy, debugging, error analysis, AI ethics, and everyday AI experiences. They argued that AI systems should provide instructional scaffolding, socio-emotional support, intuitive interfaces, and access to diverse digital tools. At the environmental level, teachers highlighted the need for flexible classroom design, reliable digital infrastructure, one-to-one devices, cloud-based platforms, systematic national AI education policy, flexible school systems, teacher capacity building, collaborative school culture, and safe-to-fail environments.

The main conclusion is that effective student-AI collaboration in K-12 requires a holistic learning design rather than simple adoption of AI tools. Teachers envisioned SAC developing through three stages: learning about AI, learning from AI, and eventually learning together with AI. The paper contributes a qualitative, teacher-centered framework for designing AI-supported learning and policy, but it does not test student outcomes or specific effects of ChatGPT-based writing feedback. Its relevance to secondary writing feedback is indirect, mainly through broader implementation considerations such as teacher preparation, AI ethics, error analysis, infrastructure, and collaboration design.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative study using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis with 10 teachers. It provides useful implementation evidence but does not estimate causal effects on student outcomes and therefore fits the qualitative/correlational yellow tier.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report student outcome effect sizes or direct impact estimates; its contribution is primarily conceptual and implementation-oriented. As a result, practical impact is plausible but empirically unclear, fitting the yellow tier.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual design and implementation of student-AI collaboration in K-12 classrooms, based on teacher perspectives across varied AI applications rather than evaluation of a single specific tool.

finding.finding_summary: Across in-depth interviews with 10 Korean leading AIED teachers, participants consistently anticipated that student-AI collaboration should support higher-order cognitive and collaborative capacities such as critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving, communication, and collaboration. These are teacher-reported design expectations and perceptions rather than measured student outcomes; no effect sizes or causal estimates were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about intended student capacities (e.g., critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, computational thinking)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that effective student-AI collaboration should include socio-emotional support, such as AI acting as an encouraging learning mate and classrooms fostering motivation, persistence, and confidence through safe-to-fail environments. These findings reflect educator perceptions about desirable supports for engagement and affect, not direct student-level impact estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about motivation, persistence, affective support, and student-AI socio-emotional interaction

finding.finding_summary: Teachers expected AI and cloud-based platforms to automate repetitive tasks and support personalization, but also warned that poor system integration could increase teacher workload, especially if outputs must be manually transferred into existing school information systems. Thus, anticipated efficiency gains were conditional and accompanied by implementation tradeoffs.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about workflow automation, platform integration, and teacher workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s strongest empirical focus is on institutional requirements for student-AI collaboration: teachers emphasized the need for systematic AIED policy, flexible school systems, teacher capacity building, collaborative culture, digital infrastructure, and privacy/security safeguards. Findings indicate substantial perceived promise for system redesign, but also significant implementation barriers and governance needs; no quantitative institutional outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on policy, governance, infrastructure, school culture, privacy, and institutional supports
